chapter: Split, hospital and decline of tap
title: What the Pretty Foot is, from Walter Beatty
summary: Green says rapid tap came from the Pretty Foot walk Walter Beatty used, and the interviewers press him to explain it as a two-partner step of invitation and caress.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: And Peckin' Joe -- I called him good buddy, too, you see, because he was a rapid tapper, see, he wouldn't have it -- he did acrobatics, you know, and we called him -- the acrobat calls it aerials, but he featured his feet, you know. Just the sound of rapid tap because it was -- it was really taken from Pretty Foot, which was some kind of walking that Walter Beatty Bailey used to do -- Pretty Foot. He was proud because he had -- his fiance had accepted him, you know, and had named the day, so he Pretty Foot -- he was walking, you know.
We did do a Pretty Foot, didn't we?
Yeah.
Did we do a Pretty Foot?
Yes.
When you did the 32 bars off Walter Bailey, you did a Pretty Foot in there.
Yeah.

Pretty Foot is more or less a walk isn't it? Not a walk -- but I mean a tap step that is not that over active. It sort of comes down from the Bo Jangles -- Pretty Foot -- it comes out of the Bo Jangles flavors?
Yeah.

I think of these things as different flavors, you know, these different dancers have their own way of making their own little flavor, you know. I mean, everybody could get a recipe for a cake, but they might do it just that
little bit different -- they might put just a little -- one might put a little more raisins in and someone else may put something else -- another kind of spice. This is find so interesting, really.
Yes, well, you see, that's because -- may I have this dance? See, that's really what Pretty Foot is taken from. Because if she --
Well what is
: Where does that again --
: If she what?
If she says -- she kind of bows and says, 'Yes?' Well, the Pretty Foot occurs after that because it's like a new love story, a new romance, you know.
: But Pretty Foot was never a two person dance -- it was a one person dance, though.
Yes, the Pretty Foot is -- of course they would ask each other and some kind of a physical language and is it going to be a twostep or a one step -- or the Porter house stomp? Or polka.

: How would you -- how would you sort of simplify so that we could understand more exactly what the Pretty Foot is? Is it just a combination of -- is it an actual walking step or is it a sort of dance step that they decided to call it Pretty Foot because of the maybe your foot would be turned out or the overall picture of the dancer when they were doing this thing when you look pretty -- prettier
than say like wing has its look, Pretty Foot has its look.

Well, the Pretty Foot is like describing your partner -- your dance partner, you see. So, that makes it -- that gives it the individuality -- like he and she, you know. He describe her as she rises and comes forward, and she describes him as she comes forth, you see. And the Pretty Foot is happening there. That makes it a two foot step, Pretty Foot, see.
Something like a mime artist trying to put over how he would say, his fiance looked or something so he --
That's it.
Or each foot represents each partner, is what you're saying.

Yeah. Each one, you see, she arises and approaches the dance floor, you see, and they have to embrace or caress and then dance, whatever it is -- whether it's a polka, one step, two step, slow drag, Porterhouse stomp, you see, or foxtrot, you see. But that was -- the two foot dancing would be occurring at this time because he's there, he don't just stand. He tells her in dance language what the tempo of the music is and which way to go, right or left, when he began. And they caressed or embraced, and that's why it's called Pretty Foot because they try to look their best, or get on the good foot, you know. See, win a prize or whatever.
